articles.title: NASA Navigation Experiment Shows Promise for Planetary Landings
articles.summary: NASA successfully demonstrated technology designed to help spacecraft autonomously navigate to safe landing sites on the Moon and on other planets. An Alta-X drone equipped with the agency’s Safe and Precise Landing – Integrated Capabilities Evolution (SPLICE) guidance, navigation, and control payload completed simulated lunar descent and landing maneuvers Aug. 27. The flight took place […]
articles.content:
An Alta-X drone flies an advanced guidance and navigation system known as the Safe and Precise Landing – Integrated Capabilities Evolution (SPLICE) experiment near NASA’s Armstrong Flight Research Center in Edwards, California, on Wednesday, July 15, 2026. Researchers at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston developed SPLICE, which successfully communicated with the remotely piloted aircraft during hover maneuvers in flight. SPLICE will help spacecraft land precisely and detect and avoid potential hazards, which is critical for NASA missions to the Moon and to Mars. NASA/Ryan Kline

NASA successfully demonstrated technology designed to help spacecraft autonomously navigate to safe landing sites on the Moon and on other planets.

An Alta-X drone equipped with the agency’s Safe and Precise Landing – Integrated Capabilities Evolution (SPLICE) guidance, navigation, and control payload completed simulated lunar descent and landing maneuvers Aug. 27. The flight took place at Rogers Dry Lake near NASA’s Armstrong Flight Research Center in Edwards, California.

During the tests, the SPLICE payload used an advanced guidance system to map the terrain and assess potential landing areas. If the system determines the targeted landing area is unsafe, the system diverts the drone to a safer location. The system generates high-resolution digital elevation maps from light-detection and sensor data.

Davis Adams, project manager, confirms that an advanced guidance and navigation system known as the Safe and Precise Landing – Integrated Capabilities Evolution (SPLICE) experiment is communicating with an Alta-X drone near NASA’s Armstrong Flight Research Center in Edwards, California, on Wednesday, July 15, 2026. Researchers at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston developed SPLICE, which successfully communicated with the remotely piloted aircraft during hover maneuvers in flight. SPLICE will help spacecraft land precisely and detect and avoid potential hazards, which is critical for NASA missions to the Moon and to Mars. NASA/Ryan Kline

Researchers at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston developed the SPLICE payload and partnered with specialists at NASA Armstrong to integrate, test, and fly it aboard the Alta-X drone in June and July. Those tests verified communications, data handling, telemetry, and command- control performance between the SPLICE payload and the drone to prepare for a full-scale test at Voyager Technologies in Mojave, California, later this month.

“This flight test is the culmination of almost a decade of work, for the SPLICE project,” said Davis Adams, NASA project manager. “This flight raised the technology readiness level, priming it for integration into future robotic and crewed lunar flights. Validation of the guidance and navigation systems are applicable to terrestrial, lunar, and Martian descent and landing missions.”

NASA has worked with a number of commercial lunar lander providers to implement iterations of SPLICE into their platforms. A number of the landers slated for upcoming Moon Base missions leverage data collected by NASA through the development of systems like SPLICE to execute soft touchdowns on the lunar surface.

Justin Link, a small uncrewed aircraft pilot, left, Justin Hall, chief pilot, and Davis Adams, project manager, test an advanced guidance and navigation system known as the Safe and Precise Landing – Integrated Capabilities Evolution (SPLICE) experiment on an Alta-X drone near NASA’s Armstrong Flight Research Center in Edwards, California, on Wednesday, July 15, 2026. Researchers at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston developed SPLICE, which successfully communicated with the remotely piloted aircraft during hover maneuvers in flight. SPLICE will help spacecraft land precisely and detect and avoid potential hazards, which is critical for NASA missions to the Moon and to Mars. NASA/Carla Thomas

“We are coordinating with industry regarding the usage of the guidance system once the system is available in the NASA software catalog, currently planned for this fall,” Adams said. “Some of the companies also are evaluating the system’s navigation capabilities for precision landing applications, as well as potential extensions for autonomous surface mobility.”

NASA’s Flight Opportunities project, based at NASA Armstrong, enabled flight testing of the SPLICE project early in its development that laid a foundation for it to continue advancing its technology readiness level to what it is today. Flight testing included both a descent altitude and a landing trajectory in 2019 similar to what is expected on a lunar mission and the demonstration of two NASA-developed precision landing sensor systems in 2020.

articles.personality_title: NASA tests new technology to help spacecraft land safely on the Moon and Mars
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – NASA has been working on a new technology to help spacecraft land safely on the Moon and other planets. Landing on these places is very tricky because the surface can be rough and full of dangers.

**What happened** – On August 27, 2026, NASA tested a system called SPLICE (Safe and Precise Landing – Integrated Capabilities Evolution) on an Alta-X drone near NASA’s Armstrong Flight Research Center in California. This system helped the drone fly and land by creating detailed maps of the ground below and choosing safe spots to land. If the system found a risky area, it moved the drone to a safer place.

**Impact** – This test shows SPLICE can help future spacecraft land more precisely and avoid hazards on the Moon and Mars. It is important because landing safely is one of the hardest parts of space missions. NASA has worked on this technology for almost ten years, and it will now be used by other companies building lunar landers for upcoming Moon missions.

**What's next step** – NASA plans to add SPLICE to its software catalog by fall 2026, making it available for other space companies to use. They will also explore how the system can help robots move safely on the surfaces of the Moon and Mars.

**One-sentence takeaway** – NASA’s successful test of the SPLICE system brings spacecraft closer to landing safely and accurately on the Moon and Mars, improving future space exploration missions.

articles.personality_title_es: La NASA prueba nueva tecnología para ayudar a las naves a aterrizar con seguridad en la Luna y Marte
articles.personality_presentation_es:

**Qué pasó** – El 27 de agosto de 2026, la NASA probó un sistema llamado SPLICE (Aterrizaje Seguro y Preciso – Evolución de Capacidades Integradas) en un dron Alta-X cerca del Centro de Investigación Armstrong en California. Este sistema ayudó al dron a volar y aterrizar creando mapas detallados del terreno y eligiendo lugares seguros para aterrizar. Esto es importante porque aterrizar es una de las partes más difíciles de las misiones espaciales. La NASA ha trabajado en esta tecnología durante casi diez años y ahora otras compañías que construyen módulos lunares la usarán en misiones futuras.

**Próximo paso** – La NASA planea incluir SPLICE en su catálogo de software para el otoño de 2026, para que otras empresas espaciales puedan usarlo. También estudiarán cómo el sistema puede ayudar a robots a moverse con seguridad en la superficie de la Luna y Marte.

articles.personality_title: Hubble Telescope Sheds Light on Oxygen Loss in Small Galaxies
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientists have been studying small galaxies called dwarf galaxies, which have fewer stars than big galaxies like our Milky Way. These tiny galaxies are important because they help us learn how galaxies change and grow over time.

**What happened** – Using NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope, researchers looked closely at 37 nearby dwarf galaxies, including one named NGC 4449. They discovered that these galaxies have much less oxygen than expected. The oxygen created by stars in these galaxies seems to be lost, likely blown away by strong winds.

**Impact** – This finding is important because oxygen is a key ingredient in understanding how galaxies develop. Knowing that dwarf galaxies lose most of their oxygen helps scientists better understand the life cycle of stars and the changes galaxies go through. It also explains why these small galaxies look different from larger ones.

**What's next step** – Scientists will continue studying more dwarf galaxies to see if this oxygen loss happens everywhere. They will also try to learn more about the winds that push oxygen out and how this affects the future of these galaxies.

**One-sentence takeaway** – The Hubble Telescope found that small dwarf galaxies lose most of their oxygen, revealing new details about how galaxies grow and change.
articles.personality_title_fr: Le télescope Hubble révèle la perte d’oxygène dans les petites galaxies
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les scientifiques étudient de petites galaxies appelées galaxies naines, qui ont moins d’étoiles que les grandes galaxies comme la Voie lactée. Ces petites galaxies sont importantes pour comprendre comment les galaxies évoluent.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Grâce au télescope spatial Hubble de la NASA, des chercheurs ont observé de près 37 galaxies naines proches, dont une nommée NGC 4449. Ils ont découvert que ces galaxies contiennent beaucoup moins d’oxygène que prévu. L’oxygène créé par les étoiles semble être emporté par de forts vents.

**Impact** – Cette découverte est importante parce que l’oxygène aide à comprendre le développement des galaxies. Savoir que les galaxies naines perdent la plupart de leur oxygène aide les scientifiques à mieux comprendre le cycle de vie des étoiles et les changements dans les galaxies.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs vont continuer à étudier d’autres galaxies naines pour voir si cette perte d’oxygène est partout. Ils chercheront aussi à comprendre comment les vents expulsent l’oxygène et ce que cela signifie pour l’avenir des galaxies.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Le télescope Hubble a découvert que les petites galaxies naines perdent la plupart de leur oxygène, révélant de nouvelles informations sur l’évolution des galaxies.
articles.personality_title_es: El telescopio Hubble revela la pérdida de oxígeno en galaxias pequeñas
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los científicos estudian galaxias pequeñas llamadas galaxias enanas, que tienen menos estrellas que galaxias grandes como la Vía Láctea. Estas galaxias pequeñas son importantes para entender cómo cambian y crecen las galaxias.

**Qué pasó** – Usando el telescopio espacial Hubble de la NASA, los investigadores observaron 37 galaxias enanas cercanas, incluyendo una llamada NGC 4449. Descubrieron que estas galaxias tienen mucho menos oxígeno del que esperaban. El oxígeno creado por las estrellas parece perderse, probablemente por fuertes vientos.

**Impacto** – Este hallazgo es importante porque el oxígeno es clave para entender cómo se desarrollan las galaxias. Saber que las galaxias enanas pierden la mayor parte de su oxígeno ayuda a los científicos a comprender mejor el ciclo de vida de las estrellas y los cambios en las galaxias.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos seguirán estudiando más galaxias enanas para ver si esta pérdida de oxígeno ocurre en todas partes. También intentarán aprender más sobre los vientos que expulsan el oxígeno y cómo esto afecta el futuro de las galaxias.

**Resumen en una frase** – El telescopio Hubble descubrió que las pequeñas galaxias enanas pierden la mayor parte de su oxígeno, mostrando nuevos detalles sobre cómo crecen y cambian las galaxias.
